title: Stratford-upon-Avon
subtitle: Shakespeare's life, walked in order
intro: How did a glove-maker's son from a family in debt climb to the top, and what did it cost him? Walk his whole life in order, through the town where it happened.

dayGlance.title: His youth
dayGlance.sub: The Birthplace, his school and Anne Hathaway's Cottage.

actsLede: One question: how did he climb to the top, and what did it cost him?

acts.label: Act 1 · Where he started
acts.tagline: A family that climbed, then fell.
acts.narrative: His father married up, became head of the town, then lost everything. William was about 12.

acts.label: Act 2 · How he learned
acts.tagline: Old stories, and his first look at theatre.
acts.narrative: Latin and the stories of ancient Rome upstairs. Travelling actors in the hall downstairs.

acts.label: Act 3 · Married at 18
acts.tagline: A wife, three children, then gone.
acts.narrative: A wife and three children by 20, then seven lost years, and London.

acts.label: Act 4 · How he got rich
acts.narrative: Called a nobody, he became an owner, won back his father's coat of arms, and bought a big house.

acts.label: Act 5 · The top, and the cost
acts.tagline: A theatre, a king, a grave, and no son.
acts.narrative: The Globe, the king, a grave by the altar. And a son who died, and a family line that ended.

acts.label: Act 6 · How his name survived
acts.tagline: His friends, a festival, and his words.
acts.narrative: His friends saved his plays, a rained-out festival made Stratford famous, and we still use his words.

planNote.text: One Birthplace ticket (£25 online, £27 at the door) also covers New Place. Add Anne Hathaway's Cottage (£5) and the Schoolroom (£10) when you book. The Birthplace has timed entry, so book ahead. To do it all in one day, start at the Birthplace at 10: New Place has the shortest hours (11 to 3 in autumn), and the church is only open on Sunday afternoons. Hall's Croft and Mary Arden's Farm are closed to visitors. Coming twice instead? Split after Anne Hathaway's Cottage: his youth on the first visit, then the rise, the end and the legend on the second.

birthplace.name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
birthplace.onCamera: This is where it all starts. William Shakespeare was born in this house in 1564. To understand everything he did later, you need to know what happened to his family while he was growing up here.
facts: His father, John, made gloves. He married Mary Arden. Her father owned land, and John's father rented his farm from him. So John married up.
And John kept climbing. He bought houses, joined the town council, and in 1568, when William was four, he became head of the town, like a mayor.

Then it all went wrong. In the 1570s, he was taken to court for selling wool without permission, and for charging too much interest on loans. He fell into debt and stopped going to council meetings. He asked for a coat of arms, a badge for upper-class families. He was refused. William was about 12.
birthplace.closeOnCamera: So that's the boy who grew up in this house. He watched his father climb to the top of this town, and then lose it all. I think he spent the rest of his life winning it back. And it started at school, five minutes away.

routeCard.note: Enter through the Shakespeare Centre on Henley Street.

see: The room where he was born
His father's glove workshop
The old timber fronts of Henley Street
planCard.todo: Timed entry, so book ahead. Open 10 to 5 from spring to autumn. Your ticket also covers New Place. Then walk to the school, about 6 minutes.

schoolroom.name: Shakespeare's Schoolroom and Guildhall
schoolroom.onCamera: This is almost certainly where Shakespeare went to school. And this building gave him two things that shaped his whole life. One was in this classroom. The other was in the hall downstairs.
facts: In the classroom, he learned Latin, six days a week. He would have read the great stories of ancient Rome. Years later, he turned some of those same stories into his own plays and poems.

Downstairs, in the town hall, travelling actors came to perform. Some of the most famous acting companies in England played here while he was a boy. And his own father, as a town leader, decided which plays they could perform.
schoolroom.closeOnCamera: So when he left school, he had two things: the old stories, and a first look at the theatre. He never went to university. That will matter later. But first, at 18, his life changed very fast, in a farmhouse a mile from here.

routeCard.note: The schoolroom is upstairs. The Guildhall, the medieval town hall, is downstairs.

see: On the way: Harvard House on High Street (1596), the family home of John Harvard's mother. Harvard University is named after him.
The Tudor schoolroom upstairs
The Guildhall downstairs
The Guild Chapel next door (free)
Timber houses from the 1400s next door, built for poor old people
planCard.todo: Open 11 to 5, last entry 4:15. £10 if you add it to your Birthplace ticket, £15 on its own. Then walk to Anne Hathaway's Cottage in Shottery, about 25 minutes.

anne-hathaway.name: Anne Hathaway's Cottage
anne-hathaway.onCamera: This is where Anne Hathaway grew up. In 1582, William married her. He was 18. She was 26, and already pregnant. A few years later, he left her and their children here, and went to London. So what happened?
facts: Their daughter Susanna was born six months after the wedding. Two years later came twins, a boy and a girl: Hamnet and Judith. So by 20, William had a wife and three children to support.

Then he disappears. For about seven years, there's no record of him at all. Historians call them the lost years. Nobody knows how he got to London. Remember those travelling actors in the town hall? Maybe he left with one of them.
anne-hathaway.closeOnCamera: However he got there, the next time we hear about him, it's 1592. He's in London, and people are laughing at him. Five years later, he was rich enough to buy one of the biggest houses in his home town. Let's go and see it.

routeCard.sub: Cottage Lane, Shottery · a mile from the centre
routeCard.note: About 25 minutes on foot from the school.

see: The thatched farmhouse
The cottage garden and orchard
planCard.todo: Open 10 to 5. £5 if you add it to your Birthplace ticket. Then walk back into the centre to New Place, about 25 minutes.

new-place.name: Shakespeare's New Place
new-place.onCamera: This is where Shakespeare's big house stood. He bought it in 1597, when he was 33. Just five years earlier, he was a nobody in London. So how did he get rich so fast? Not by writing plays.
facts: In 1592, a jealous writer called him an 'upstart crow'. He meant: a nobody. A small-town actor with no university education, who thought he could write as well as them.

Then a plague closed London's theatres. When they opened again in 1594, he made the smartest move of his life. He didn't just write for an acting company. He became one of its owners. Now he got a share of all the money, not just pay for his writing.

Two years later, in 1596, he did what his father never could. He got his father the coat of arms he had been refused twenty years before. The Shakespeares were officially upper class now. And the next year, he bought this house.
new-place.closeOnCamera: So that's how he did it. He didn't just write the plays. He owned part of the business. And he won back everything his father had lost. The house is gone now: a later owner knocked it down in 1759, after a fight with the town over tax. But Shakespeare wasn't finished. He was about to climb even higher.

routeCard.note: Enter by the gate on Chapel Street.

see: The garden where the house stood
Nash's House next door: the home of Thomas Nash, who married Shakespeare's granddaughter Elizabeth
planCard.todo: Included in your Birthplace ticket. Check the hours: in autumn it's open 11 to 3. Then walk to Holy Trinity, about 7 minutes.

holy-trinity.name: Holy Trinity Church: the top
holy-trinity.onCamera: By the end of his life, Shakespeare had climbed higher than anyone in his family could have dreamed. He owned part of the most famous theatre in London. He worked for the king. And he's buried here, next to the altar. Let me show you how he got each of those.
facts: In 1598, the man who owned the land under their theatre wanted them out. So while he was away for Christmas, the company took the whole theatre apart. They carried the wood across the river, and built the Globe. Shakespeare owned part of it.
In 1603, the new king, James the First, made Shakespeare's company his own. They became the King's Men. Shakespeare was now a servant of the king, and he was given red cloth for a royal uniform.
And in 1605, he paid £440, a huge amount then, for a share of the money this church collected. That gave him the right to be buried inside, next to the altar. Most people were buried outside.
holy-trinity.closeOnCamera: So the glove-maker's son ended up with a theatre, a king, and a grave by the altar. He died in 1616, at 52. Look at the stone. It says: 'Cursed be he that moves my bones.' In other words: don't touch my bones. But this church tells another story too. A sadder one.

routeCard.note: Go in by the avenue of lime trees.

see: On the way: Hall's Croft, where his daughter Susanna lived with her husband, Dr John Hall. They married in this church in 1607.
The avenue of lime trees
His grave and the curse
His monument on the wall
planCard.todo: Hours change with the day and the season, and on Sundays it's only open in the afternoon. The grave costs £5. It's a working church, so keep your voice down. Stay for the next part, here at the grave.

river.name: The statue by the river
river.onCamera: His family died out. But 400 years later, people come here from all over the world because of him. So how did his name survive? It took three things: his friends, a festival that went badly wrong, and his words.
facts: First, his friends. Seven years after he died, two actors from his company printed his plays in one big book, the First Folio. Eighteen of the plays had never been printed before, including Macbeth and The Tempest. Without his friends, we'd probably have lost them.

Then, in 1769, the most famous actor in Britain held a three-day festival here for Shakespeare. It rained non-stop, and not one Shakespeare play was performed. But it worked. After that, people started coming to Stratford to see where he lived. And they still do.
And his words. 'Green-eyed monster.' 'A wild-goose chase.' 'It's all Greek to me.' We still say these today, and they come from his plays.
river.closeOnCamera: His family is gone. But his words are still here, in the way we talk, 400 years later.

routeCard.note: Your opening and closing lines are here too.

see: On the way: the Royal Shakespeare Theatre on the river
The statue: Shakespeare with four of his characters. Hamlet; Lady Macbeth; Falstaff, a fat, funny knight; and Prince Hal, a young prince who becomes king.
The narrowboats in the canal basin
Clopton Bridge, built around 1484 by Hugh Clopton, the same man who built New Place
planCard.todo: Your opening and closing lines are here too. Bridgeway car park is about 3 minutes away.

holy-trinity-cost.name: Holy Trinity Church: the cost
holy-trinity-cost.onCamera: His children were baptised in this church. And in 1596, the same year he got his coat of arms, he buried his only son here. To understand what that meant to him, you need to know one thing about a coat of arms. It passes from father to son.
facts: His son, Hamnet, died at 11. We don't know how. Now the family badge Shakespeare had worked so hard for had no son to pass to.
A few years later, he wrote a play called Hamlet. Back then, Hamnet and Hamlet were almost the same name. Nobody knows if he was thinking of his son. But it's hard not to wonder.

In 1616, a month before he died, he changed his will. His daughter Judith had just married a man caught in a scandal. So Shakespeare made sure that man couldn't take her money. He was still protecting the family.
holy-trinity-cost.closeOnCamera: He left almost everything to his daughter Susanna, and then to her sons. But she had no sons. His last grandchild died in 1670, with no children. The family he built all this for came to an end. His name didn't. So how did it survive?

routeCard.note: Same place, the next part of the story.

see: The family graves in a row beside his: his wife Anne, his daughter Susanna and her husband
planCard.todo: Then walk along the river, past the theatre, to his statue in Bancroft Gardens, about 10 minutes.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: Everyone knows this man as a poet. But here's what most people don't know. He was a glove-maker's son, and his family fell into debt when he was a boy. By the end of his life, he was rich, he worked for the king, and he was buried next to the altar. How did he do it? And what did it cost him? Today I'm walking through his life, in order, in the town where it happened.

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: So that's his story. A glove-maker's son who watched his family fall, and spent his life climbing back. He won the money, the badge and the king. He lost his son, and his family line. But not his name. If you enjoyed this, please like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.
